instruction: Describe an old friend you didn't contact for a long time and got in contact with again.
response: I'd like to talk about how I recently reconnected with my old friend Lisa, whom I hadn't spoken to in almost six years. We first met in high school and became inseparable almost immediately — we bonded over a shared love of books and films, and we'd spend hours debating plot twists or swapping novel recommendations. But after graduation, life pulled us in different directions. She went to university in another city, and although we promised to stay in touch, the messages gradually became fewer and farther between until, eventually, they stopped altogether. It wasn't a falling-out or anything dramatic — we simply drifted apart, which, thinking about it now, is somehow even sadder. Then, a few months ago, her profile popped up on my social media feed, and on a whim, I sent her a message saying it had been far too long. To my delight, she replied almost immediately, and it was as if no time had passed at all. We ended up chatting for nearly three hours that first evening, filling each other in on everything — her career, my job, relationships that had come and gone, even how our old classmates were doing. A couple of weeks later, we met up in person at a café, and honestly, within five minutes we were laughing about the same old inside jokes from high school. What struck me most was how much I'd genuinely missed her — not just the conversations, but her humour and the way she completely understood me. Since then, we've made a pact to meet at least once a month, and it feels wonderful to have her back in my life. This whole experience taught me a valuable lesson: that some friendships are worth reviving no matter how much time has passed, and that a simple message is sometimes all it takes to bridge years of silence.

instruction: Describe a person who always has strong opinions.
response: The person who springs to mind when I think of strong opinions is my colleague, Mark, whom I've worked with for the past four years. Mark is the kind of person who never sits on the fence about anything — politics, design choices, even something as trivial as where the team should go for lunch — and he'll voice his view with total conviction, whether you asked for it or not. I first noticed this trait during a project meeting early on, when he flat-out disagreed with our manager's strategy in front of everyone. Most of us were stunned into silence, but he calmly laid out his reasoning, point by point, and to everyone's surprise, his argument actually held up. As for why he's like this, I think it comes down to the fact that he's exceptionally well-read and follows current affairs closely, so he rarely expresses an opinion without evidence to back it up. He's also just naturally confident, perhaps to the point of stubbornness at times. Honestly, his strong opinions are a double-edged sword. On one hand, they can be a bit overwhelming — meetings with him can turn into lengthy debates, and he doesn't always realise when to let an issue go. A few of my more reserved colleagues find him intimidating and try to avoid discussions with him altogether. On the other hand, I genuinely value his honesty in a workplace where most people tend to say what's safe rather than what they actually think. He often raises points nobody else has considered, and he's forced me to sharpen my own arguments more than once. Over the years, I've learned that the trick with Mark is to engage with him seriously rather than dismiss him, because underneath the bluntness, he's fair-minded and will happily concede if you prove him wrong. Love him or loathe him, team discussions are certainly never dull with him around.

instruction: Describe a person who has chosen a career in the medical field.
response: I'd like to talk about my cousin Lisa, who has chosen probably the most demanding career path imaginable — she's a doctor working in the emergency department of a large hospital. We grew up in the same neighbourhood and were close from an early age, so I've witnessed her entire journey firsthand. What's interesting is that her decision wasn't born out of family pressure or prestige — it came from experience. When she was in high school, she volunteered at a local hospital, and seeing firsthand how good medical care could transform patients' lives left a deep impression on her. She often tells the story of an elderly patient she befriended there, whose recovery after surgery inspired her to dedicate her life to medicine. Getting there was anything but easy. The medical programme took years longer than a normal degree, the exams were relentless, and there were times when she was so exhausted and stressed that she considered giving up. I remember her practically living in the library during exam season, surviving on instant noodles and about five hours of sleep a night. Even now, as a qualified doctor, the sacrifices continue — she works gruelling shifts, including nights and holidays, and she's missed more than one family gathering because of an emergency call. And yet, she never complains. When I ask her how she copes, she says that the moment a patient recovers and walks out of the ward makes every sleepless night worthwhile. I honestly feel immense admiration and pride when I think about her. She's chosen a path defined by service and sacrifice rather than convenience, and she does it with genuine compassion, not just technical skill. To me, she represents the very best of what a career in medicine should be, and whenever I'm tempted to complain about my own workload, I remind myself of what she handles every single day.

instruction: Describe a person who likes to make things by hand (e.g. toys, furniture).
response: I'd like to talk about my friend Emily, who is one of the most gifted hands-on creators I've ever met. She loves making things by hand — everything from knitted toys and leather keyrings to small pieces of furniture like bookshelves and wooden stools. Her flat honestly looks like a cross between a craft studio and a workshop, with shelves of fabric, jars of buttons, and her trusty sewing machine taking pride of place by the window. I first discovered her talent when she gave me a handmade phone case for my birthday — beautifully stitched, perfectly sized, and honestly nicer than anything I could have bought in a shop. When I asked her why she devotes so much time to it, she gave me an answer that's stuck with me. She said that in a world where everything is mass-produced and identical, making something with your own hands gives it a soul. She finds the whole process deeply therapeutic, too — after a stressful day at work, she'll spend hours absorbed in a project, and she says it clears her mind better than any screen ever could. What impresses me most is her patience and precision. I once watched her restore a battered old chair she'd picked up at a flea market — sanding it, repairing the joints, reupholstering it — and weeks later it looked like a designer piece. She's even started selling some of her creations at weekend craft markets, and they sell out surprisingly fast. Beyond the practical skills, I think her hobby reflects a wonderful mindset: she values quality over quantity, cherishes things that last, and finds joy in the process rather than just the result. Whenever I visit her workshop, I come away inspired, and she's actually got me attempting my first woodworking project — a small bookshelf — which, I'll admit, is testing my patience to its very limits.

instruction: Describe a person who likes to read a lot.
response: The person I'd like to describe is my friend Sarah, who is without question the most avid reader I've ever known. Reading isn't just a hobby for her — it's as essential as breathing. She always carries a book in her bag, and if she's ever waiting for a bus or standing in a queue, out it comes. Her tastes are impressively broad, but her great loves are mystery novels and historical fiction — she devours everything from Agatha Christie to sweeping sagas set centuries ago, and she's currently working her way through the classics as well. I got to know her reading habits properly in university, where we shared a dormitory, and I have vivid memories of her staying up until two in the morning because she 'just had to finish one more chapter'. She owns a towering bookshelf — actually, several of them — crammed with hundreds of volumes, and she treats them like old friends, re-reading her favourites every year. What I find remarkable is how much she retains. She can discuss the fall of the Roman Empire, the politics of Victorian England, or forensic investigation techniques with surprising authority, all picked up from novels. Conversations with her are never dull because she's constantly sharing fascinating tidbits: 'Did you know that...' is practically her catchphrase. When I've asked her why she reads so much, she says books allow her to live a thousand lives instead of one — she can walk the streets of ancient Rome one week and solve a murder in a sleepy English village the next. She also insists that reading helps her unwind after stressful days far better than scrolling on her phone ever could, and honestly, I believe her, because she's one of the calmest, most articulate people I know. She's actually inspired me to read more myself; I've managed four books this year thanks to her recommendations, which, for me, is something of a personal record.

instruction: Describe a place in your city where you have seen wild animals.
response: The place I'd like to describe is Green Park, a large nature reserve on the outskirts of my city, which is surprisingly rich in wildlife despite being only a short drive from the urban centre. I first discovered it a few years ago when a colleague recommended it as a weekend walking spot, and it's become one of my favourite places to unwind ever since. The park covers a huge area of woodland, grassland, and several small lakes, and because it's been protected from development, the animals there behave as if humans are merely guests in their home. On my visits, I've spotted squirrels darting up tree trunks, rabbits grazing at the edge of meadows in the early morning, and on one unforgettable occasion, a family of deer crossing a quiet path just a few metres in front of me — we all stood frozen, watching each other, before they melted gracefully back into the trees. Birdwatchers absolutely love the place; there are herons standing motionless by the water's edge, woodpeckers drumming on old trunks, and countless smaller birds I couldn't name but love to listen to. If you're patient and quiet, you might even glimpse a fox at dusk. I usually go there on weekend mornings with my camera, and I've learned that the trick is to arrive early — the park does get busy with families and joggers later in the day, and the wildlife keeps a lower profile when there are crowds. What I cherish most about the place is the feeling it gives me: standing in the middle of a forest, hearing nothing but birdsong and rustling leaves, it's easy to forget a city of millions is just beyond the trees. In an age when green spaces are constantly shrinking, I think a place like Green Park is a genuine treasure, and I feel fortunate to have it within reach. I'd honestly recommend it to anyone needing to reconnect with nature.

instruction: Describe an ideal and perfect place where you would like to stay, e.g. a house or an apartment.
response: My ideal place to live would be a house by the sea, somewhere along the southern coast of Spain, where the climate is warm and sunny for most of the year. I've pictured it in my head so many times that I could probably draw the floor plan from memory. It wouldn't be a grand mansion — just a modest, single-storey house with whitewashed walls, terracotta roof tiles, and large floor-to-ceiling windows that frame the ocean and let the golden light flood in. The moment you step inside, you'd see an open-plan living space with a modern kitchen at one end and a cosy reading nook by the window at the other, complete with a deep armchair and a stack of books I never get around to finishing. The centrepiece, though, would be the balcony — wide and deep, furnished with a couple of rattan chairs and a small table for morning coffee, overlooking a garden full of jasmine, bougainvillea, and a lemon tree or two. My favourite feature, without question, would be a private stone path leading directly down to the beach, so I could take a barefoot walk along the shore every morning before the day begins. I imagine the rhythm of life there would be wonderfully simple: watching the sunrise with a cup of tea, working with the sound of waves in the background, and ending each day with dinner on the terrace as the sky turns pink. More than anything, this place appeals to me because I'm at my calmest near water. The sea has this incredible ability to put everything in perspective — problems seem smaller, and time seems slower. Of course, I know it's a dream that requires a lot of saving and planning, but that's precisely what makes it a good motivation. Having a clear picture of where I want to end up makes the hard work feel meaningful, and one day, I fully intend to make that little white house a reality.

instruction: Describe a crowded place you've been to.
response: One of the most unbelievably crowded places I've ever experienced is the Great Wall of China during the Golden Week holiday last October. I'd gone with a group of university friends, and we'd deliberately chosen the autumn because we'd heard the foliage around the Wall was spectacular — reds and golds stretching across the mountains. What we failed to account for, rather stupidly in hindsight, was that tens of millions of other people had exactly the same idea. The journey there was our first warning: the traffic approaching the site crawled at walking pace, and the car park looked like an ocean of tour buses. But nothing quite prepared us for the Wall itself. From the entrance, the walkway was a solid river of people — visitors from every corner of China and, it seemed, every corner of the world, packed shoulder to shoulder. At the most popular sections and photo spots, the queue moved at a shuffle, and getting a picture without a dozen strangers in the background was practically an Olympic sport. I remember laughing with my friends at one point because, for a full ten minutes, we barely moved at all — we were simply carried along by the crowd. Surprisingly, though, the experience wasn't ruined by any of this. The moment you looked up from the sea of heads and took in the view — the Wall snaking endlessly over misty mountain ridges as far as the eye could see — all the discomfort seemed to evaporate. There's a reason it's one of the wonders of the world, and no crowd can diminish that. If anything, the sheer number of people added something to the atmosphere: a shared sense of awe. That said, the trip did teach me a lasting lesson about travel planning — never, under any circumstances, visit a major Chinese landmark during a national holiday unless you enjoy queuing more than sightseeing. Next time, we're going in November, on a weekday, at dawn.

instruction: Describe a cultural place that you would like to learn the culture there.
response: A cultural place I'm genuinely longing to visit is the Louvre Museum in Paris, and it's been at the top of my wishlist ever since I studied art history in secondary school. Of course, I've known about the Louvre for as long as I can remember — it appears in textbooks, films, and documentaries — but the more I've learned about it, the more I've wanted to experience it in person rather than through a screen. For those unfamiliar, it's the world's largest and most visited art museum, housed in a former royal palace in the heart of Paris, instantly recognisable by the glass pyramid at its entrance. Its collection spans thousands of years and countless civilisations — Egyptian antiquities, Greek sculptures, Islamic art, and of course the great European paintings, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. What fascinates me most is the opportunity to understand European culture at its roots. I'm particularly drawn to the French Renaissance period and the way art from that era reflects the social and political upheavals of its time — you can trace the changing values of an entire society just by walking through the galleries in chronological order. I'd want to do more than simply glance at famous masterpieces; I'd want to join a guided tour, learn the stories behind each work, and understand why certain pieces became cultural landmarks. Friends who've visited tell me that photographs simply cannot capture the scale and detail of the paintings — the Mona Lisa, they say, is smaller than expected, while some of the vast canvases are overwhelming in person. Beyond the art itself, I'm drawn to the building: the palace architecture, the history of the kings who lived there, and the contrast between the classical facade and the modern pyramid. To me, the Louvre represents humanity's creative achievements gathered in one place, and spending even a single day there — though frankly, you'd need a week — would be an unforgettable education in itself.

instruction: Describe someone's room where you enjoy spending time.
response: The room I enjoy spending time in most is my friend Anna's bedroom, which I honestly consider the cosiest space I've ever set foot in. I first visited when we started university together and I came over to borrow some notes — I remember thinking immediately that stepping into her room felt like stepping into a warm hug. The first thing you notice is the colour scheme: soft terracotta and cream walls, which she painted herself, paired with warm fairy lights draped around the window frame that give the whole room a gentle golden glow in the evenings. There's a comfortable sofa in the corner piled high with knitted cushions and a chunky blanket, positioned perfectly for both chatting and lazy afternoon naps. Along one wall stands her greatest treasure — an enormous bookshelf, packed with novels arranged partly by author and partly, she admits, by 'vibes'. She's an art student, so there's also a small wooden desk by the window covered with sketchbooks, paints, and half-finished projects, and watching her work there, absorbed and humming to herself, is oddly calming. My favourite feature, though, is the large window that looks out onto her landlady's garden — in spring it's a riot of cherry blossoms, and in autumn the leaves turn copper and gold. We've spent countless evenings there: reading in companionable silence, dissecting our week over mugs of tea, or doing nothing more ambitious than watching the rain streak down the glass. What makes the room so special, I've realised, isn't really the decor at all — it's that the space reflects Anna herself: warm, creative, and completely unpretentious. It's her sanctuary, and she generously shares it. Whenever my own flat feels stressful or cluttered, I find myself suggesting we study at her place, because honestly, all my worries seem to dissolve somewhere between that sofa and the fairy lights.

instruction: Describe a public garden or park.
response: The public space I'd like to talk about is East Coast Park, a large seaside park not far from where I live, and honestly the pride of our neighbourhood. It stretches for kilometres along the coastline, so no matter how many people visit, it never feels stifling — there's always another quiet stretch of grass or a hidden bench waiting to be found. What makes it special is its location right by the sea. There's a constant fresh breeze coming off the water, and if you pause and listen, you can hear the rhythmic sound of waves washing against the shore, which instantly melts away whatever stress you brought with you. The park is fantastically well designed, too. A wide cycling and jogging track runs the entire length of it, and on weekends it's buzzing with families on rented bicycles, joggers, and skaters weaving between beach volleyball games and picnic blankets on the grass. There are barbecue pits you can book, plenty of shaded pavilions, and a row of small seafood restaurants near the eastern end where people gather to watch the sunset over dinner. My own routine is to go there once or twice a month, usually on a Saturday evening. Sometimes I cycle the full length of the park and back, sometimes I just spread a mat on the grass with a book, and quite often I end up doing neither and simply watching the ships on the horizon while the sky changes colour. What I love most is how the park brings the whole community together — you hear several languages, see every generation, from toddlers chasing pigeons to elderly couples doing tai chi at dawn. In a fast-paced city where everyone seems glued to their screens, East Coast Park is that rare place where people genuinely slow down, breathe, and enjoy the moment, and I feel lucky to have it practically on my doorstep.

instruction: Describe a small shop or store you often go to.
response: The small shop I'd like to describe is a family-run bakery just around the corner from my apartment, called Sunshine Bakery, though everyone in the neighbourhood simply calls it 'old Mr. Lin's'. It's barely five minutes from my front door, tucked between a dry cleaner's and a fruit stall, and you'd walk past it without a second glance if you didn't know what you were missing. I stumbled upon it about two years ago when I followed the smell of fresh bread down the street one morning, and I've been a loyal customer ever since — I stop by once or twice a week, usually on my way to work, for a coffee and whatever pastry has just come out of the oven. The shop itself is tiny, with only a handful of tables, but it's spotless and warmly lit, with shelves packed with steamed buns, egg tarts, crusty loaves, and their famous red bean buns, which regularly sell out by mid-morning. What keeps me coming back, though, goes beyond the food. Mr. Lin and his wife run the place themselves, and they know their regulars by name and by order — after my third visit, Mrs. Lin was already bagging my usual sesame bun before I'd said a word. If you arrive early enough, you'll catch Mr. Lin's son, a university student, helping out before class, and the whole family has this easy warmth that makes even a two-minute visit feel personal. Their prices are refreshingly reasonable, too — noticeably cheaper than the chain cafés nearby — and the quality is incomparably better because everything is baked fresh on site each morning at dawn. I make a point of supporting them because I genuinely believe small shops like theirs are the heartbeat of a neighbourhood; they give it character and human connection that no supermarket ever could. Frankly, the thought of that little bakery disappearing one day is enough to make me want to buy an extra bun every visit.

instruction: Describe the most expensive item you have ever bought.
response: The most expensive item I've ever purchased is my laptop, which set me back the best part of two months' salary when I bought it about a year ago from an electronics store in Beijing. It wasn't an impulse buy by any stretch — I deliberated for weeks, watched countless comparison videos, and read more reviews than I'd care to admit before finally committing. The reason I was willing to invest so heavily was practical: I work as an IELTS teacher, and my old laptop had become a genuine obstacle. It was painfully slow, the battery died within an hour, and it crashed mid-lesson more than once, which was mortifying when I was teaching an online class. I needed a machine I could rely on completely. So I chose a model with a powerful processor, a high-resolution display, and generous storage — features that matter enormously when you're juggling video calls, editing teaching materials, and running multiple programmes simultaneously. And I use it constantly: lesson planning in the mornings, online classes through the day, video editing for my educational channel in the evenings — it's essentially the hub of my working life. Was it worth the eye-watering price tag? Unreservedly, yes. The difference has been night and day — tasks that used to take ages now take minutes, and I've completely stopped worrying about it failing at a crucial moment. Having said that, the purchase did teach me a lot about spending decisions. I learned to distinguish between price and value: the laptop was expensive, but measured in hours of work saved and frustration avoided, it's arguably the best value thing I own. It also taught me to save and plan for big purchases rather than rushing them. Nowadays, whenever I'm tempted by something costly, I ask myself whether it will genuinely improve my daily life — and if the answer is no, I walk away, because that laptop set a pretty high standard for what 'worth it' really means.

instruction: Describe a traditional food at a traditional festival or a special event in your country.
response: The traditional food I'd like to talk about is mooncakes, the iconic treat of the Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, when the moon is at its fullest and brightest. Mooncakes are small, dense, round pastries, usually about the size of a palm, with a thin, golden-brown crust and a rich, thick filling inside. The classic fillings are lotus seed paste or red bean paste, often with a salted duck egg yolk nestled in the centre — the yolk symbolises the full moon itself. The tops are beautifully decorated with intricate stamped patterns, typically featuring characters for longevity or harmony, which makes each cake look almost too pretty to eat. The tradition behind them is what I find most touching. The Mid-Autumn Festival is fundamentally about family reunion, and sharing mooncakes under the full moon — cutting them into small wedges so everyone gets a piece — is a symbolic act of togetherness and completeness. I have warm memories of every festival from my childhood: the whole family gathering at my grandparents' house, the table laden with mooncakes, pomelos and tea, and my grandfather telling the legend of Chang'e, the woman who floated to the moon, while we gazed upward hunting for the jade rabbit's outline in its craters. Nowadays the tradition has evolved wonderfully — there's a friendly rivalry every year over which flavours are best, from the classic lotus paste to avant-garde creations like ice-skinned mooncakes with mango or even chocolate fillings. Honestly, mooncakes are so rich that most people can only manage a small slice, but that's rather the point — they're not really about quantity. To me, the taste of a mooncake is inseparable from the feeling of the festival: family crammed around one table, laughter, full stomachs, and that enormous orange moon rising over the rooftops. It's edible nostalgia, really.

instruction: Describe a picture or photo in your home that you like.
response: The photo I'd like to describe is a framed family picture that hangs in our living room, and it's unquestionably my favourite image in the whole house. It was taken about five years ago during a rare family holiday to a seaside town — rare because, with my parents' work schedules and my siblings' studies, getting all five of us in one place at the same time is roughly as likely as winning the lottery. In the photo, we're standing on the beach in the late afternoon, all of us mid-laugh, with the sunset painting the sky in brilliant streaks of orange and pink behind us. My dad took the picture himself, arms outstretched with the camera, after persuading a passing stranger to gather us all together — and somehow he managed to hold the camera perfectly level while grinning at the same time. What makes the photo special to me isn't professional composition; in fact, by photography standards it's delightfully imperfect — my sister's hair is windswept across her face, and my brother is caught blinking. But those little flaws are exactly why I love it. It captures something no staged portrait ever could: a genuine moment of happiness. That holiday was one of the last times we were all carefree together — soon afterwards, I moved away for university, my sister started working, and family holidays became a thing of the past, or at least a thing of group chats and scheduling apps. I chose the living room wall for it deliberately, because that's where the whole family gathers, and I wanted the photo to watch over our reunions. Guests always ask about it, and it inevitably sparks an hour of 'remember when' storytelling. To me, that frame holds more than a photograph — it holds a reminder that the best moments in life are simple ones: a beach, a sunset, and the people you love standing beside you.

instruction: Describe an online video where you learned something new.
response: I'd like to talk about an online video that genuinely taught me something valuable — a cooking tutorial I stumbled upon on YouTube about a month ago. It was a weekend afternoon, and I'd just burnt yet another batch of fried rice, which frankly was the last straw. Out of frustration, I searched for basic cooking techniques, and up came a video by a professional chef titled something like 'Ten mistakes every beginner cook makes'. It ran about twenty minutes, and I ended up watching it twice in a row, taking notes like I was back in school. The content was wonderfully practical. The chef started with knife skills — how to hold the knife properly, how to curl your fingers to avoid slicing them off, and how to chop an onion efficiently without weeping over it. Before this video, my chopping technique could best be described as 'enthusiastic but dangerous'. He then moved on to the fundamentals I'd never considered: why pasta water should taste like the sea, why meat needs to rest after cooking, and most importantly, the principle of mise en place — preparing and organising all your ingredients before the heat even goes on. That single idea has transformed my cooking; I used to panic-chop garlic while my onions turned to charcoal, and now everything flows calmly. I applied the lessons immediately, cooking that very evening, and the difference was remarkable — even my flatmate, a notoriously harsh critic, went back for seconds. What made this video stand out from the thousands of others was the chef's teaching style: no flashy editing or exaggerated reactions, just clear explanations of the 'why' behind each technique, demonstrated slowly and repeated when it mattered. It genuinely boosted my confidence in the kitchen and saved me from many future kitchen disasters. Since then, I've subscribed to his channel and worked through several more tutorials, and I'd honestly recommend the approach to anyone who cooks, or attempts to.

instruction: Describe a challenge you faced that you thought was rather difficult.
response: One of the toughest challenges I've ever faced was delivering a presentation in English at an international conference in Shanghai last year. Let me set the scene: I'd been studying English for well over a decade, and I was comfortable reading academic papers and even chatting with foreign colleagues. But standing up in front of an audience of several hundred people — a large proportion of them native speakers and experts in my field — was an entirely different beast. The invitation had come months earlier, and my initial excitement quickly curdled into dread as the date approached. Every night, I rehearsed in front of my mirror, recorded myself on my phone, and cringed at every stumble. My inner critic grew louder by the day: What if I mispronounce a key term? What if they ask a question I can't understand, let alone answer? The week before the conference, I genuinely considered inventing an excuse to withdraw — a cold, a family emergency, anything. What stopped me was remembering how I'd felt when the invitation first arrived: it was recognition, an opportunity most people in my position would jump at. So I threw myself into preparation instead — I refined my slides relentlessly, rehearsed answers to every question I could imagine being asked, and even hired a tutor for two mock presentation sessions. On the day itself, my heart was hammering so hard I could feel it in my ears as I walked to the podium. But somewhere around the third slide, something shifted: I stopped performing and started communicating, and the audience nodded along, laughed at my joke, and even seemed engaged. The Q&A session went better than I'd dared hope — I answered every question, and one researcher even asked for my contact details afterwards. Walking off that stage, I felt ten feet tall. That experience taught me a lesson I'll never forget: confidence isn't something you wait to feel — it's something you build by doing the very thing that terrifies you.

instruction: Describe a prize you have received.
response: The prize I'm proudest of is the finisher's medal from my first full marathon, which I completed in Beijing in the autumn of 2021. It hangs on a hook by my desk, and honestly, no trophy I've ever won means more to me. To explain why, I need to go back about a year before the race. I was, to put it kindly, not a runner. Climbing three flights of stairs left me wheezing, but something about turning thirty made me desperate to prove to myself that I could still set an ambitious goal and actually achieve it. So, perhaps foolishly, I signed up for a full marathon — all 42.195 kilometres of it. The training that followed was humbling. It started with short, shuffling three-kilometre jogs that left my legs aching for days. Over the months, I built up gradually: five kilometres, then ten, then the endless weekend long runs that devoured entire Sunday mornings. I trained through summer heat and pouring rain, battled blisters, and mentally negotiated with myself on more than one occasion to just quit. The race day itself was an emotional rollercoaster. The first half flew by on pure adrenaline, buoyed by cheering crowds and my fellow runners. But by kilometre thirty, I hit the infamous 'wall' — my legs turned to lead, every step was an argument between my body and my will, and I genuinely doubted I could finish. What carried me through was breaking the remaining distance into tiny goals — just reach the next lamp post, then the next water station — and the incredible support of strangers shouting encouragement. Crossing that finish line, I burst into tears, a bizarre mix of pain, disbelief, and overwhelming joy. The medal itself is simple — a ribbon and a disc of metal — but to me it represents something far greater: months of discipline, every early morning when I chose training over sleep, and the discovery that I'm far more resilient than I ever believed. That's why it remains my most treasured prize.

instruction: Describe a film that you watched recently.
response: The film I'd like to talk about is Oppenheimer, the historical drama directed by Christopher Nolan, which I watched at the cinema with a friend just a few weeks ago. The film chronicles the life of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist who led the Manhattan Project — the secret American programme that developed the atomic bomb during the Second World War. I'll be honest: I went in with fairly modest expectations, figuring it would be a standard biopic, but I came out completely floored. What struck me first was the intensity of the storytelling. Rather than a straightforward timeline, Nolan weaves together different periods of Oppenheimer's life — his early academic years, the wartime project in Los Alamos, and the political hearings that haunted him afterwards — and the tension builds relentlessly towards the Trinity test, the first detonation of the bomb. When that moment came, the cinema fell utterly silent; you could have heard a pin drop. What elevated the film beyond entertainment for me was its central moral question: what responsibility do scientists bear for how their discoveries are used? Oppenheimer famously recalled the Bhagavad Gita after the explosion — 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds' — and the film doesn't shy away from his torment. One scene in particular, where he visualises the horror his creation could unleash, has stayed with me ever since. Cillian Murphy's performance is extraordinary; he conveys entire oceans of guilt and ambivalence with little more than his eyes. Walking out of the cinema, my friend and I talked for over an hour about science, ethics, and war — surely the mark of a great film. It also prompted me to read more about the actual history afterwards, which I'd highly recommend doing. I'd say Oppenheimer is a must-watch for anyone who enjoys thought-provoking cinema, though be prepared: it's long, dense, and it will sit in your mind for days.

instruction: Describe a time when you answered a phone call from someone you didn't know in a public place.
response: I'd like to describe the time I answered a phone call from a complete stranger in a public place, which turned into one of those small, oddly memorable life episodes. It happened last month at a quiet café near my office, where I'd settled in with a coffee and a novel, savouring a rare peaceful afternoon. My phone buzzed with a call from an unknown number, and on autopilot, I answered. A woman's voice, urgent and slightly flustered, launched straight into conversation — no greeting, no introduction. She asked if she was speaking to 'John' and said she'd been trying to reach him all day about a matter she described as very urgent. I quickly clarified that she had the wrong number and I'd never met any John in my life. There was a pause, and then a mortified apology — but here's where it got interesting: instead of hanging up immediately, she seemed reluctant to end the call, explaining she'd been anxiously waiting on this call all afternoon because it concerned her friend's hospital appointment. We ended up chatting for a couple of minutes, and I did my best to reassure her that her friend John was probably fine, that phones die and numbers get mistyped, and that she should try the clinic directly. She thanked me warmly, sounding genuinely calmer, and we hung up. What made the episode memorable was the setting: the café was one of those hushed, laptop-and-latte establishments where everyone pretends not to listen but absolutely does. I was painfully aware of heads lifting over laptops as my half of the conversation became progressively stranger — 'No, I'm not John... a hospital?... well, I hope he's okay' — and I felt my ears turning red. Looking back, it was a small, slightly awkward moment, but it left me with a warm feeling. It reminded me that behind every wrong number is a real person with real worries, and that even a stranger's two minutes of patience can genuinely help.

instruction: Describe something that made you feel confident.
response: The experience that did more for my confidence than anything else was delivering a major presentation at work last year, in front of not just my team but several senior managers. The stakes were high: I'd been working on a project analysis for weeks, and I'd been chosen to present the findings — the first time the company had entrusted someone at my level with such a visible role. I prepared obsessively. I researched until I knew the material inside out, rehearsed in front of my mirror until the words felt natural, and even roped my flatmate into playing the role of a hostile senior manager asking difficult questions. I still remember the night before, lying awake running through the opening lines on a loop. On the day, standing outside the meeting room, my heart was pounding and my palms were clammy — I actually considered asking a colleague to swap with me. But once I stepped up, plugged in my laptop, and delivered my first sentence, something remarkable happened: the preparation took over. My voice steadied, the slides flowed, and I found myself genuinely enjoying the explanation rather than merely surviving it. By midway, I was making eye contact around the room, and I noticed the managers nodding — actually nodding. The real test came in the Q&A, when one director posed a pointed question about my cost projections. To my own surprise, the answer came to me instantly, backed by the exact data I'd studied. He smiled and said, 'Good — you've clearly done your homework.' Coming from him, that was high praise indeed. After the meeting, my manager told me the presentation had changed how the leadership saw me. But the deeper change happened internally: I walked out of that room knowing, not hoping, that I could communicate under pressure. That single experience restructured how I see myself professionally, and it's why I now volunteer for opportunities I once would have dodged. Confidence, I learned, isn't a personality trait — it's evidence, accumulated one challenge at a time.

instruction: Describe a time when you lost a valuable item.
response: I'd like to talk about the time I lost my wallet while travelling in Guangzhou last winter — an experience that turned my stomach into a knot and taught me a lasting lesson about vigilance. The wallet itself wasn't extravagantly expensive, but it was precious to me: besides around 500 yuan in cash, it held my ID card, several bank cards, and — most painfully — a small photo of my family that I'd kept with me for years. I discovered the loss at the worst possible moment: standing at the ticket gate of Guangzhou railway station, reaching into the outer pocket of my bag where I'd carelessly stowed it earlier, and finding nothing but empty fabric. I can still recall that cold drop in my stomach as I frantically emptied the entire bag onto a bench — books, charger, umbrella — and watched no wallet emerge. In a panic, I retraced my every step: back through security, where I'd been juggling my laptop and jacket while rushing for a train; along the platform; even asking the station staff to check lost and found, my heart leaping each time my phone rang with an unknown number. Nothing. The logical explanation is that during the chaos at security, with a queue pressing behind me, it slipped out of that shallow pocket — a mistake I've never made before or since. In the end, I had to cancel my bank cards, and a kind colleague helped me sort out temporary travel arrangements, but the loss of that little family photo stung far more than the money. Oddly, though, the experience changed me for the better. I now use a wallet with a zip, keep it in an inner pocket, and do a quick 'wallet, phone, keys' check whenever I leave any place. It's a small ritual, but one born of a genuinely stressful day — and honestly, I've never lost anything since.

instruction: Describe a time when you asked someone for advice.
response: A time when I asked someone for advice that really mattered was about two years ago, when I was wrestling with a major career decision and turned to my mentor, Mr. Chen. At the time, I'd been offered a position at a new company — a role that excited me enormously but came with real uncertainty: a younger organisation, a steeper learning curve, and none of the comfortable predictability of my current job. I was paralysed between two fears: fear of regret if I stayed in my comfort zone, and fear of failure if I jumped. I'd spent weeks making endless mental lists that only seemed to grow longer, and I was getting nowhere. Knowing that Mr. Chen had navigated several career transitions himself — and, more importantly, that he'd always been honest with me even when the truth was uncomfortable — I asked if I could pick his brain over dinner. What impressed me about our conversation was how he handled it. He didn't tell me what to do; instead, he asked questions I hadn't thought to ask myself. What did I actually want my work life to look like in five years? Was I staying because of genuine opportunity, or simply because the familiar feels safe? What was the realistic worst-case scenario if the new job didn't work out — and could I live with it? Then he shared his own story of a botched career move, complete with all the painful details, which paradoxically made me feel much better: it reminded me that even wise people make wrong turns and survive them. His final piece of advice was simple but powerful: choose the option you'd regret not trying more, because regret over inaction tends to linger longer than failure. That reframe settled it for me. I took the new job, and looking back, it was one of the best decisions I've ever made. Beyond the career outcome, the experience taught me the true value of seeking advice — not for answers, but for better questions.

instruction: Describe a party that you enjoyed.
response: I'd like to describe a party I genuinely enjoyed — the surprise birthday party we threw for my best friend last month at a rooftop café overlooking the city. The preparation was half the fun, honestly. Our friend group spent weeks plotting in a private chat, carefully coordinated so she'd suspect nothing: her boyfriend was tasked with luring her there with the flimsy cover story of 'a quiet dinner for two', while the rest of us handled decorations, the cake, and her family, who'd quietly travelled in from another city. The venue was perfect — a small rooftop café with strings of fairy lights overhead, a gentle breeze, and the glittering skyline spread out below as the sun went down. About twenty of us squeezed in, crouching behind furniture and shushing each other like conspirators, and when she finally walked up those stairs and we all yelled 'Surprise!', her reaction was absolutely priceless: she froze mid-step, hands over her mouth, and then — to everyone's delight — burst into tears. Happy tears, thankfully. What followed was one of those evenings that remind you why friendships matter. We ate far too much — the cake was a spectacular three-layer chocolate thing her sister had secretly baked — played ridiculous party games that had us all in stitches, and went around the circle sharing favourite memories of her, which got embarrassingly emotional at times. There was a moment, maybe halfway through, when I looked around at everyone laughing under those fairy lights — her parents chatting with her university friends, two entirely separate worlds mingling effortlessly — and I felt genuinely grateful. What made the party special wasn't anything elaborate; it was the thoughtfulness behind it and the unmistakable love in the room. She later told us it was the best birthday she'd ever had, and judging by the dozens of photos she posted and the group chat that's still active weeks later, none of us have quite stopped talking about it either.

instruction: Describe a time when you helped your family member.
response: I'd like to talk about a time I helped a family member — when I supported my younger sister through her university entrance exams last year. For context, in our education system these exams are make-or-break; they largely determine which university you can attend and, in many ways, shape the opportunities that follow. My sister is bright, but she'd been struggling badly with mathematics, and the pressure was visibly wearing her down. She'd become quiet at the dinner table, complained of headaches, and I once found her in tears over a practice paper. I remembered all too well how suffocating that stress had felt when I sat the same exams years earlier, so I decided I couldn't just stand by and watch her drown. From that point on, I dedicated my evenings to her. We set up a study routine together: I sat with her every night after dinner, working through practice questions one by one, and more importantly, breaking down the concepts she'd only half-understood at school. I quickly realised her real problem wasn't ability — it was that she'd missed some fundamentals early on, so everything built on them felt like a foreign language. So we went back to basics, filling those gaps patiently, chapter by chapter. I also made her teach problems back to me, because explaining something exposes exactly what you don't understand. Beyond the academics, I tried to lift the emotional weight: I reminded her that one exam doesn't define her worth, made sure she took proper breaks, and forced her to stop revising by ten o'clock each night. The payoff came on results day: she scored higher in maths than either of us had dared hope, and got into her first-choice university. Watching her scream with joy on the phone to our parents is a memory I'll keep forever. For me, the experience was deeply rewarding — it strengthened our bond enormously, and it taught me that the best help you can give someone is patience, consistency, and belief in them.

instruction: Describe an occasion when you received good service from a company or shop.
response: I'd like to describe an occasion when I received genuinely excellent service — at a small electronics store near my office a few months ago, when I went looking for a new laptop. I'd been putting off the purchase for weeks, dreading the usual experience: a pushy salesperson steering me towards the priciest model on the shelf, spraying jargon at me and glazing over the moment I asked a technical question. So I walked into this store braced for battle, and instead, I got a masterclass in what customer service should look like. The employee who helped me — a man in his thirties with an air of someone who genuinely loved technology — started the conversation by asking about me rather than his commission: what I used my current laptop for, what frustrated me about it, what my budget realistically was. When I explained my needs — teaching online classes, editing videos, juggling multiple programmes — he didn't immediately point at the flagship machine. Instead, he talked me through three options at different price points, honestly explaining the trade-offs of each, and at one point actually steered me away from a model I'd been leaning towards, saying that for my usage I'd be paying extra for specs I'd never use. In an industry where upselling is practically an Olympic sport, that honesty stunned me. He also demonstrated everything patiently, answered my endless questions without a trace of condescension, and even took the time to transfer my files and set up the device properly. Two weeks later, when I had a minor software question, he remembered my purchase and sorted it out over the phone in five minutes. I've since recommended that store to at least four colleagues, and two of them have bought laptops there on my word alone. That experience taught me that great service isn't about flashy extras or discounts — it's about honesty, expertise, and treating the customer's interests as your own. And it's why I'll never buy electronics anywhere else.

instruction: Describe a person who loves to buy something with low prices.
response: I'd like to talk about my aunt, Lisa, who is without doubt the most enthusiastic bargain hunter I've ever come across. She's in her early fifties, works as a school secretary, and while she's certainly not short of money, she genuinely gets a kick out of snapping up a good deal. Whenever there's a sale or a discount coupon floating around, she's the first to know about it. She spends a fair amount of time comparing prices online, flicking through promotional leaflets, and even negotiating with vendors at the local market, which I find quite impressive, to be honest. I remember one particular occasion when she managed to buy a brand-name winter coat at seventy per cent off simply because she'd been tracking its price for months and pounced the moment it dropped. What's fascinating about her is that she doesn't just shop cheaply for the sake of it — she's actually rather sensible about it. She'll only buy things she genuinely needs, but she refuses to pay full price for anything if she can possibly avoid it. She often jokes that money saved is money earned, and thanks to her thrifty habits, she's been able to afford some lovely holidays and even help out family members financially from time to time. Being around her has definitely rubbed off on me. Before, I used to buy things on impulse, but now I tend to pause and ask myself whether I could get the same item elsewhere for less. I really admire her because she's turned what could be a boring chore — shopping — into something almost like a sport, and she never once comes across as stingy. If anything, she's taught me that being frugal is about being smart with your resources rather than depriving yourself, and I think that's a lesson that will stay with me for life.

topic: a person you are happy to know
instruction: Describe a person you are happy to know.
response: The person I'm genuinely delighted to know is my colleague and close friend, Mr. Zhang, who teaches mathematics at the same school as me. We first crossed paths about five years ago when we were assigned to share an office, and what started as small talk over coffee has blossomed into one of the most meaningful friendships of my adult life. What strikes people immediately about him is his incredible patience and warmth. No matter how hectic the day gets, he never loses his temper, and he has this remarkable ability to make everyone around him feel heard and valued. He's the sort of person who remembers tiny details — the name of your childhood pet, or the fact that you once mentioned liking a particular type of tea — and that thoughtfulness means a great deal. Beyond his personality, he's also tremendously generous with his knowledge. When I was struggling with a new teaching curriculum a couple of years ago, he stayed behind after work on numerous occasions to walk me through it, never once making me feel silly for asking questions. Outside of work, he's a keen photographer, and he's taught me a lot about capturing light and composition on our weekend outings. What I appreciate most, though, is his outlook on life. He firmly believes that small, consistent acts of kindness shape a person's character far more than grand gestures, and he certainly practises what he preaches. Whenever I'm feeling down or overwhelmed, a short conversation with him somehow puts everything back into perspective. Honestly, knowing him has made me a calmer and more patient person myself, because his positive energy is genuinely contagious. In a world where people are often too busy to slow down, having a friend like him is something I never take for granted, and I consider myself incredibly lucky to have met him.

instruction: Describe an actor/actress that you admire.
response: The actor I admire most is undoubtedly Tom Hanks, an American actor who has been a household name for several decades now. I first came across him when I watched Forrest Gump as a teenager, and I was completely blown away by how convincingly he portrayed a character so different from himself. Since then, I've seen many of his films, from Apollo 13 to Cast Away, and each performance has only deepened my respect for him. What sets him apart, in my view, is his extraordinary versatility. He can make you laugh out loud in a comedy and then move you to tears in a drama, often within the same film. In Cast Away, for instance, he spends a huge portion of the movie alone on a deserted island, talking to a volleyball, and yet he somehow holds your attention completely — that, to me, is the mark of a truly gifted actor. Beyond his talent, though, what I really admire is his reputation off-screen. By all accounts, he's one of the nicest people in Hollywood: humble, down-to-earth, and famously kind to crew members and fans alike. In an industry that's often associated with arrogance and scandal, he's managed to maintain a spotless image over forty years, which speaks volumes about his character. He's also known for being selective about his roles, choosing meaningful stories rather than chasing blockbuster paychecks. On a personal level, watching his films has actually shaped how I think about perseverance and humanity. His characters tend to be ordinary people who face extraordinary circumstances with quiet dignity, and there's something deeply inspiring about that. If I could meet any celebrity, he'd probably be top of my list, not because of his fame, but because he seems like someone who'd have fascinating stories and genuine wisdom to share.

instruction: Describe an interesting old person you’ve met.
response: I'd like to describe an interesting old person I met called Mr. Wang, who I came across about two years ago at a community centre in my neighbourhood. He was a retired history teacher who had taught for over thirty years, and he was volunteering as a guide at a local history exhibition, which was where our paths first crossed. What drew me to him initially was the way he spoke about the past — not as a dry list of dates and facts, but as a living, breathing story full of ordinary people's triumphs and struggles. I ended up chatting with him for well over an hour, and I remember walking away feeling genuinely enriched. Since then, we've become quite friendly, and I often drop by to listen to his stories over a cup of tea. He's full of fascinating anecdotes about what life was like in his youth — things you simply can't find in textbooks, like how people celebrated festivals decades ago or how the whole neighbourhood used to share meals during hard times. What impresses me most, though, is his attitude towards life. Despite being in his late seventies, he's incredibly open-minded and curious. He learned to use a smartphone on his own, he follows current affairs closely, and he even took up watercolour painting after retirement, something he'd dreamed about for years. He once told me that the moment you stop learning is the moment you start ageing, and that has really stuck with me. Spending time with him has changed how I view older people; rather than seeing them as fragile or out of touch, I now see them as living libraries full of wisdom and experience. I honestly hope that when I reach his age, I can face life with the same curiosity, humour, and grace that he does every single day.

instruction: Describe a person who thinks music is important.
response: I'd like to talk about my friend Sarah, who is someone for whom music isn't just a hobby — it's practically a way of life. We met at university, where we were both members of the music club, and from the very first week I could tell that she saw the world through a musical lens. She plays the piano and the guitar beautifully, and she's always humming something or tapping out a rhythm, even during ordinary conversations. What makes her stand out is how deeply she believes in the power of music. She often says that music is a universal language that can express what words simply cannot — joy, grief, longing, hope. Whenever any of us was going through a rough patch at university, she'd put together a playlist tailored to exactly what we were feeling, and somehow it always helped more than any advice could have. She's also convinced that music brings people together, and she practises what she preaches. She organised open-mic nights at our campus, encouraged people who had never performed before to get on stage, and created this wonderfully supportive atmosphere where nobody was judged. I remember being terrified the first time I sang in front of a crowd, but her encouragement got me through it, and it ended up being one of my favourite memories from university. What's more, she's now pursuing this passion professionally — she works as a music therapist, using songs to help patients with anxiety and memory problems, which I find genuinely inspiring. Being around her has definitely changed my own relationship with music. I used to treat it as background noise while studying or commuting, but thanks to her, I've learned to really listen — to notice the layers, the lyrics, the emotion woven into a piece. I think that's the mark of a person who truly believes in something: they make you believe in it too.

topic: a role model for young people
instruction: Describe someone (e.g. a famous person) who is a role model for young people.
response: The famous person I'd choose as a role model for young people is Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani education activist. I first learned about her through her autobiography, 'I Am Malala', and later through the numerous interviews and speeches she's given, and her story has stayed with me ever since. For those who may not know, Malala grew up in the Swat Valley in Pakistan, where the Taliban had banned girls from attending school. Instead of staying silent, she spoke out publicly about every child's right to an education, writing a blog for the BBC when she was just eleven years old. In 2012, when she was only fifteen, she was shot in the head on her way home from school — an attack that was intended to silence her. Remarkably, she survived, and rather than being intimidated, she came back even stronger. At seventeen, she became the youngest person ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and she continues to campaign for education through the Malala Fund. What makes her such an outstanding role model, in my opinion, is that she demonstrated extraordinary courage at an age when most of us were worrying about exams and friendships. She stood up for her beliefs even when it put her life in danger, and after everything she went through, she holds no bitterness — instead she champions peace, dialogue, and forgiveness. She's also refreshingly down-to-earth: she talks about ordinary teenage things like struggling with university coursework and arguing with her brothers, which makes her incredibly relatable for young people. I think her example teaches a powerful lesson — that you don't need to be wealthy or powerful to change the world; you just need conviction and the willingness to use your voice. If more young people followed even a fraction of her determination and compassion, the world would undoubtedly be a better place.

instruction: Describe someone who gave you encouragement.
response: The person who gave me the most meaningful encouragement in my life is my mentor, Mr. Chen, who was my professor during my university years and has remained a guiding figure ever since. I met him in my second year when I took his course, and unlike many lecturers who simply deliver their material and leave, he genuinely cared about how his students were developing, both academically and personally. The encouragement I remember most vividly came during my final year, when I was applying for a competitive scholarship that I was convinced I had no chance of winning. I'd actually talked myself out of applying and was ready to give up before I'd even started. When he found out, he didn't just give me a pep talk — he sat down with me, went through my application draft line by line, pointed out my strengths that I'd completely overlooked, and reminded me that rejection is never as costly as regret. He told me something I still think about today: that self-doubt is usually loudest right before a breakthrough. With his support, I applied, and to my astonishment, I was shortlisted and eventually won. But honestly, the scholarship itself mattered less than the confidence that whole experience gave me. What makes his encouragement special is that it's never empty flattery. He's honest about your weaknesses, but he frames them as things you can work on rather than fixed limitations, and that approach has shaped how I handle setbacks to this day. Even now, years after graduating, whenever I'm facing a difficult decision or doubting myself, I drop him a message, and his replies are always measured, thoughtful, and surprisingly encouraging. I genuinely believe that one encouraging teacher can change the trajectory of a student's life, because that's exactly what he did for mine, and I hope one day I can pass that same kind of support on to someone else.

instruction: Describe a place (indoor or outdoors) that’s suitable for study.
response: The place I'd like to describe is the local library in my neighbourhood, which I honestly believe is the perfect spot for studying, whether indoors or outdoors. It's a modest, two-storey building surrounded by a beautifully maintained garden, and it's only a ten-minute walk from my home, which makes it incredibly convenient. Inside, the atmosphere is exactly what you'd hope for: it's quiet without being stuffy, the lighting is soft and easy on the eyes, and there are comfortable reading desks arranged near large windows that let in plenty of natural light. Each desk has its own reading lamp and power outlets, so I can use my laptop without worrying about the battery dying halfway through a study session. The second floor is reserved for silent study, and there's an unspoken agreement among everyone there to respect the peace, which I really appreciate. What makes it even better is that the facilities are excellent — free Wi-Fi, an extensive collection of reference books, and even private study rooms you can book for group discussions when you're preparing a presentation with classmates. But the real gem is the garden outside. During spring and autumn, when the weather is pleasant, there are shaded benches beneath the trees where I sometimes take my notes and study al fresco. There's something about fresh air and birdsong that makes memorising vocabulary or brainstorming ideas far more enjoyable than being cooped up indoors. Another thing I love is the staff — they're friendly and helpful, and if you need a particular book or resource, they'll go out of their way to track it down for you. Compared to studying at home, where I'm constantly tempted by my bed, the fridge, and my phone, the library gives me a sense of focus and routine. Whenever I sit down at one of those desks, my mind automatically switches into study mode, and that's why it remains my favourite place to hit the books.

topic: a city for a short stay
instruction: Describe a city where you would like to stay for a short time.
response: The city I'd love to stay in for a short time is Kyoto, Japan, and it's been sitting at the top of my travel wishlist for years now. I'm planning to go there with my best friend, who shares my fascination with Japanese culture and history, and we're hoping to spend about a week there. What draws me to Kyoto specifically is that it offers something quite rare: the chance to step back in time while still enjoying all the comforts of a modern city. It was the imperial capital of Japan for over a thousand years, and you can feel that history everywhere you go. I've read so much about places like the Fushimi Inari shrine with its thousands of vermillion torii gates winding up the mountainside, the Golden Pavilion reflected in its mirror-like pond, and the famous bamboo grove in Arashiyama, where the sunlight filters through the swaying stalks. Apparently, early morning is the best time to visit these spots to avoid the crowds, so I'm already imagining dragging my friend out of bed at dawn to catch that magical atmosphere. Beyond the sightseeing, I'm really keen on experiencing the cultural side of Kyoto — trying a traditional tea ceremony, wandering through the Gion district where you might catch a glimpse of a geisha hurrying to an appointment, and staying in a ryokan, a traditional inn with tatami floors and futons. And of course, the food is a huge draw: Kyoto is famous for its kaiseki cuisine, which is a beautifully presented multi-course meal, as well as street food at Nishiki Market. What I love about the idea of a short stay, rather than living there permanently, is that it would feel like a truly immersive escape — a week of quiet temples, cherry blossoms if we time it right, and completely different rhythms of life. I honestly can't think of a better destination for a memorable short trip.

instruction: Describe a city/town/village (not your hometown) you would like to live in.
response: The place I'd love to live in is Vancouver, a coastal city on the west coast of Canada, and it's somewhere I've dreamed of settling down in ever since I watched a documentary about it a few years ago. What immediately strikes people about Vancouver is its unique blend of urban convenience and breathtaking nature. On one hand, it's a thoroughly modern city with excellent public transport, world-class universities, and a thriving job market, particularly in technology and film. On the other hand, you're never more than twenty minutes from the mountains, the ocean, or a forest trail, which is something very few cities in the world can offer. I imagine my typical weekend there would involve cycling around the seawall at Stanley Park — which is supposedly one of the most beautiful urban parks anywhere — hiking in the North Shore mountains, or simply watching the sunset over English Bay. Another thing that appeals to me is the city's incredible multicultural character. It's one of the most diverse cities in North America, so I'd have no trouble finding authentic food from every corner of the world, and people there are known for being friendly and welcoming to newcomers. The climate is another plus, at least compared to the rest of Canada: while the winters are rainy, they're remarkably mild, so you escape the brutal snowstorms that other Canadian cities endure. Of course, I'm aware it's not perfect — Vancouver has a reputation for being one of the most expensive cities in the country, especially when it comes to housing, which would definitely be a challenge. But for me, quality of life is about more than property prices. The chance to live somewhere I could go skiing in the morning and walk along the beach in the afternoon, while enjoying a relaxed, health-conscious lifestyle, is incredibly appealing. Vancouver really does seem to offer the best of both worlds, and that's exactly why it tops my list.

instruction: Describe a place you’ve been to where things are expensive.
response: The place I'd like to talk about is the Ginza district in Tokyo, Japan, which is without question the most expensive place I've ever set foot in. I visited it a couple of years ago during a trip to Japan, and honestly, nothing quite prepared me for the sheer opulence of the area. As I strolled through the immaculate, tree-lined streets, I was surrounded by flagship stores of virtually every luxury brand you could name — Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Dior — with elaborate window displays that looked more like works of art than shop fronts. The buildings themselves were architectural statements, gleaming glass towers housing jewellery boutiques, art galleries, and department stores that have been operating for over a century. What really brought home just how expensive the place was, though, was a rather humbling experience I had at a department store food hall. I picked up what I assumed was an ordinary gift box of strawberries, only to turn the price tag over and discover they cost the equivalent of fifty dollars — for a single box! And that wasn't even the most extravagant item on the shelf; there were melons selling for well over a hundred dollars each, individually wrapped and presented like precious jewels. Even a simple cup of coffee at a café there cost several times what I'd normally pay back home. To be fair, you could sense the quality in everything — the service was extraordinarily polished, with staff bowing as you entered every shop, and even the packaging was exquisite. But as a budget traveller, I mostly enjoyed Ginza the way you'd enjoy a museum: window shopping, soaking up the dazzling atmosphere, especially in the evening when the neon billboards lit up the whole district. My wallet was grateful when I left, but I don't regret the visit one bit — it gave me a fascinating glimpse into a world of luxury I'd never experienced before.

instruction: Describe a place you visited where the air was not clean.
response: I'd like to describe a place I visited where the air quality was genuinely shocking — an industrial city I travelled to for a business trip about two years ago. I'd heard that air pollution was an issue there, but reading about it and actually experiencing it are two completely different things. The moment I stepped off the plane, I noticed a thick, greyish haze hanging over everything, blurring the skyline and muting the colours of the buildings. It wasn't long before I could feel it physically too: within hours, my throat felt scratchy, my eyes were watering, and the air had a faint smell of burning coal and exhaust fumes that never quite went away. During my three days there, I don't think I saw the sun clearly once — it was just a pale, washed-out disc behind the smog. Locals told me that on the worst days, visibility dropped so much that you could barely make out buildings a few streets away, and that schools would keep children indoors during breaks. What struck me most was how people had simply adapted to it. Many wore face masks as routinely as we wear watches, air purifiers hummed in every home and office, and apps showing the air quality index were checked as often as the weather forecast. I have to admit, I found it quite depressing — even my morning jog, which I usually love when travelling, was out of the question. The whole experience made me reflect on the environmental cost of rapid industrialisation and how easy it is to take clean air for granted. When I flew back home and breathed in that first lungful of fresh air, it genuinely felt like a luxury. Since then, I've become much more conscious of environmental issues, and I've developed real sympathy for the millions of people around the world who have no choice but to live with polluted air every day.

instruction: Describe a tourist attraction that very few people visit but you think it is interesting.
response: The tourist attraction I'd like to describe is a hidden gem in my region called Qingyan Ancient Town, which, despite its incredible charm, remains remarkably under-visited compared to the country's famous destinations. It's an ancient fortress town perched in the hills about an hour's drive from the provincial capital, originally built as a military garrison over six hundred years ago during the Ming Dynasty. What makes it so special, in my opinion, is its wonderful sense of authenticity. Unlike some heavily commercialised ancient towns where every other shop sells identical mass-produced souvenirs, Qingyan still feels like a living, breathing place. Locals actually reside there, and you can watch everyday life unfold: elderly residents playing chess on weathered stone benches, artisans hand-making traditional snacks in doorways, and elderly women in traditional dress chatting on moss-covered steps. The architecture is stunning — stone walls, carved wooden windows, and winding cobbled lanes that lead to ancient temples, a former monastery, and well-preserved city gates with watchtowers offering panoramic views over the surrounding countryside. One of my favourite discoveries there was a tiny family-run shop that has been making rose sugar for generations, following a recipe that supposedly dates back centuries. The town is also surrounded by dramatic karst hills and terraced fields, so even the journey there is scenic. The reason so few tourists visit, I suspect, is simply that it lacks the name recognition of places like the Great Wall or West Lake, and it isn't heavily promoted in travel guides. But honestly, that's part of its appeal — you can explore at your own pace, chat with locals, and actually hear the birds rather than tour buses. I visited with a couple of friends last autumn, and we all agreed it was the highlight of our trip. It's exactly the kind of place I hope never changes, and I'd recommend it to anyone seeking genuine cultural depth over crowds.

instruction: Describe an unusual meal that someone made for you.
response: I'd like to describe an unusual meal that my grandmother made for me during the winter holidays when I was around ten years old, and even now, decades later, it still brings a smile to my face. That year, the whole family had gathered at her house for the Spring Festival, and there were more of us at the table than usual — over a dozen relatives crammed into her modest dining room. My grandmother, being the wonderful cook she was, had spent days preparing the traditional feast, but here's the thing: she'd accidentally run out of several key ingredients because of the sheer number of people, and the shops were closed for the holiday. Rather than panic, she did what resourceful women of her generation always did — she improvised. What she created was a sort of everything-but-the-kitchen-sink dumpling filling: minced pork mixed with chopped cabbage, finely diced water chestnuts for crunch, dried mushrooms she'd been saving for a special occasion, and even a handful of pickled mustard greens that added a surprising tangy kick. Honestly, by any conventional standard, the combination sounded completely bizarre, and some of my cousins were openly sceptical when the plates came out. But the moment we all took our first bite, there was this collective silence followed by everyone scrambling for seconds. The flavours somehow worked together perfectly — savoury, a little sweet, with that unexpected hint of tanginess — and my grandmother looked absolutely triumphant, as if she'd planned it all along. She christened them her 'lucky dumplings' and joked that they'd bring fortune because they were made from whatever the kitchen gave her. What makes the meal so memorable to me isn't just the taste, though. It was the laughter around that crowded table, the story we still retell at every family gathering, and the lesson my grandmother taught us without even trying: that creativity and love are the real secret ingredients in any dish.

instruction: Describe a piece of technology you own that is difficult to use.
response: The piece of technology I'd like to talk about is my smartwatch, which, ironically, is supposed to make my life simpler but has proven surprisingly difficult to use. I bought it about a year ago, lured in by all the hype about fitness tracking and productivity features, and I have to admit the sleek design and glowing reviews convinced me it would be a game-changer. Well, was I in for a rude awakening. The trouble started right from the setup process, which required downloading three different apps, creating an account on yet another platform, and pairing the device through a menu that seemed deliberately buried. It took me the better part of an evening just to get the thing connected to my phone. Once it was up and running, the complications continued. The touchscreen is so sensitive that merely adjusting my sleeve triggers functions I never asked for, and the interface is so crammed with icons and swipe gestures that I'm constantly stumbling into features I didn't know existed. Notifications are another headache — by default, the watch mirrors every single alert from my phone, so during meetings it would buzz insistently for emails, group chats, and even likes on social media posts, which was mortifying. I've spent hours digging through settings menus trying to customise it, and just when I think I've tamed it, a software update comes along and rearranges everything. To make matters worse, the fitness tracking isn't even accurate; it once logged my fifteen-minute walk to the bus stop as a vigorous cycling session, which frankly made me question its intelligence.
