Interestingly, some of these struggles are generational — my younger cousin set it up and navigated it effortlessly in ten minutes flat, which made me feel my age. Despite all this, I keep wearing it, mainly out of stubbornness and the sunk cost of what I paid for it. It has taught me a valuable lesson, though: more features don't necessarily mean a better user experience.

instruction: Describe something you own and want to replace now.
response: The item I've been meaning to replace is my laptop, which has been my faithful companion for the past eight years but is now quite honestly on its last legs. I bought it during my first year at university, and at the time it was a decent mid-range machine that handled everything I threw at it — essays, research, films, the occasional game. In a way, it's been through everything with me: all-nighters before exams, my first freelance projects, even the pandemic years when it became my window to the outside world. However, age has certainly caught up with it. The battery, which once lasted a full working day, now dies within forty minutes unless it's plugged in, which essentially turns my 'portable' computer into a desktop that lives permanently tethered to a wall socket. It takes the best part of five minutes to boot up, and opening more than a couple of browser tabs makes the fan roar like a jet engine taking off. I've also had a couple of alarming moments recently — the screen has started flickering occasionally, and just last month it froze completely in the middle of an important video call, which was beyond embarrassing. I have done what I can to keep it going: I upgraded the hard drive to an SSD a couple of years ago, which gave it a new lease of life, and I regularly clean out files and uninstall programs to keep it from choking. But there's only so much you can do when the core hardware is that outdated. The main reason I haven't replaced it yet is simply that I've been waiting for the right time financially, and, I'll admit, a certain sentimental attachment — it feels almost ungrateful to abandon a machine that served me so loyally for so long. Still, I know the day is coming soon, and I'm already researching energy-efficient, lightweight models that would suit my current needs much better.

instruction: Describe an important plant in your country.
response: The plant I'd like to talk about is the tea plant, which is undoubtedly one of the most culturally and economically significant plants in my country. Tea has been cultivated here for thousands of years, and it's woven into almost every aspect of daily life. The tea plant itself is an evergreen shrub with glossy, dark green leaves and small white flowers that bloom delicately when the season is right. It thrives in regions with mild temperatures, abundant rainfall, and well-drained, slightly acidic soil, which is why it's typically grown on hillsides and in mountainous areas — the famous tea-producing regions are often breathtakingly beautiful, with endless rows of tea bushes tracing the contours of the slopes like green velvet. The most prized leaves are the tender young buds picked in early spring, and the picking is still largely done by hand, which is a skill passed down through generations. What makes the tea plant so important, though, goes far beyond agriculture. Economically, the tea industry supports millions of people, from farmers and pickers to traders and tea house owners, and it's a major export that carries our country's name around the world. Culturally, tea is the heartbeat of social life. Offering a cup of tea is how we welcome guests, apologise, show respect to elders, and seal agreements — there's even a saying that the first thing offered in any home should be tea. The traditional tea ceremony, with its emphasis on patience, mindfulness, and appreciation of subtle flavours, has become a symbol of our national identity. Personally, I grew up watching my grandfather brew tea every morning with almost ceremonial care, and to this day, the smell of freshly brewed tea instantly reminds me of those quiet mornings. I honestly can't imagine our country without it — the humble tea plant isn't just a crop here; it's a thread that runs through our history, economy, and everyday rituals.

instruction: Describe a new law that you would like to see/introduce in your country.
response: A new law I'd genuinely like to see introduced in my country is mandatory recycling legislation, which would require every household and business to separate their waste properly. Let me explain what I mean. Under this law, all residents would be legally obliged to sort their rubbish into clearly defined categories — recyclables like paper, glass, metal, and plastic, organic waste such as food scraps, and general rubbish — with designated collection bins and schedules for each. Businesses, especially restaurants and retailers, would face even stricter requirements, and there would be meaningful penalties for repeat offenders, perhaps starting with warnings and escalating to fines. I imagine the government would also need to invest in the infrastructure to support it: more recycling facilities, standardised colour-coded bins in every neighbourhood, and public education campaigns to teach people exactly what goes where, because honestly, many people don't know that a greasy pizza box can't be recycled. The reason I feel so strongly about this is that our current voluntary system simply isn't working. Landfill sites are filling up at an alarming rate, and I've read that a huge proportion of what ends up buried could actually be recycled or composted. We've all seen the images of rivers choked with plastic waste, and it's becoming impossible to ignore the connection to climate change and environmental degradation. I know some people argue that such a law would be inconvenient or hard to enforce, but I'd point to countries like Japan, South Korea, and Germany, where strict waste-sorting rules have been in place for years and where citizens now sort their rubbish almost instinctively. Of course, the law would need to be phased in gradually, with plenty of support rather than just punishment, so people don't feel overwhelmed. But I truly believe that a bit of short-term inconvenience is a small price to pay for cleaner cities, reduced pollution, and a healthier environment for the next generation.

instruction: Describe a sport you’ve watched/seen and you would like to try.
response: The sport I'd love to try is rock climbing, which I first became fascinated by after watching documentaries and videos of climbers scaling breathtaking cliff faces in spectacular locations around the world. I've never actually done it myself — the closest I've come is an indoor climbing wall I stared at longingly at a fitness centre — but it's been on my bucket list for years now. What initially captured my imagination was the combination of physical challenge and mental puzzle that climbing represents. From what I've read, it's not just about raw strength; it's often described as a physical chess game, where you have to read the wall, plan your route several moves ahead, and figure out the most efficient way to use each handhold and foothold. I find that appeals to me far more than repetitive gym workouts, where frankly I lose motivation after ten minutes on the treadmill. There's also the obvious attraction of being outdoors. I picture myself eventually climbing on real rock, high above a valley, with fresh air and stunning views as a reward for the effort — apparently the sense of achievement when you reach the top of a difficult route is absolutely addictive. Of course, I'm under no illusions about the demands of the sport. It requires serious grip strength, flexibility, and core stability, none of which I currently possess in abundance, so I'd need to start with beginner courses at an indoor climbing gym. Safety is another aspect I'd want to take seriously — learning proper belaying techniques, double-checking equipment, and always climbing with experienced partners, because it's definitely not a sport to approach casually. Interestingly, I've heard that climbing has become increasingly popular recently, even making its Olympic debut, so there are now plenty of facilities and communities for newcomers. I'm actually planning to sign up for a beginner's course next month with a colleague who shares the same interest, and I genuinely can't wait to finally give it a proper go.

instruction: Describe an advertisement you’ve seen that you didn’t like.
response: I'd like to talk about an advertisement I really disliked, which was a TV commercial for a fast-food chain promoting one of their new burgers. I first came across it while watching a popular drama series in the evening, when unfortunately the ad was aired during every single break. The commercial itself followed a formula that seems to be everywhere these days: glossy, slow-motion shots of a burger that looked suspiciously perfect — cheese stretching impossibly far as the patty was pulled apart, lettuce so vibrantly green it practically glowed, and steam rising in artful curls. All of this was set to upbeat, extremely catchy music, with an energetic voiceover making claims like 'the most delicious burger you'll ever taste' and urging viewers to try it immediately. Now, you might wonder why something so seemingly harmless bothered me so much. First of all, the exaggeration was blatant. Anyone who has ever eaten at a fast-food restaurant knows the actual product looks nothing like the advertised version — the real burger is squashed, lopsided, and generally rather sad-looking. Secondly, the ad was aimed squarely at children and young people, using bright colours, cartoon mascots, and toys included with the meal, which I find quite irresponsible given rising concerns about obesity and unhealthy eating habits. To make matters worse, the repetition was relentless — I must have seen that same commercial a dozen times in a single evening, and it got to the point where I could recite the slogan word for word, which I suspect was exactly the advertisers' goal. What frustrated me most was the realisation that enormous sums of money had been spent on making unhealthy food look glamorous while offering no genuinely useful information whatsoever. It actually put me off the chain completely, which I suppose is the opposite of what they intended. Since then, I've become much more sceptical of advertising in general, and I tend to mute ads or skip them whenever possible.

instruction: Describe a website you often visit.
response: The website I'd like to talk about is Reddit, which is a social news aggregation and discussion platform that I've been using regularly for several years now. I first discovered it through a friend at university who recommended it as a goldmine for finding information on literally any topic imaginable, and he was absolutely right — I was hooked almost immediately. For those unfamiliar with it, Reddit is essentially a collection of thousands of individual communities called 'subreddits', each dedicated to a specific interest, and users post questions, stories, links, and discussions that others can vote up or down. What I love most about it is the sheer breadth of what's on offer. I'm a member of communities about cooking, personal finance, language learning, and travel, and each one has its own distinct personality and standards. Whenever I have a problem — whether it's a technical glitch, a recipe question, or advice about a big life decision — I can almost always find someone who's dealt with exactly the same issue and is willing to share their experience in detail. The voting system is clever because it naturally pushes the most helpful and insightful answers to the top, while low-quality comments sink into oblivion. Of course, it's not without its flaws. Like any open platform, there's plenty of misinformation and the occasional heated argument, so you have to read critically and double-check anything important. There's also the danger of losing track of time entirely — I've lost more evenings than I'd care to admit to scrolling through fascinating threads about history or science. But on balance, it has genuinely enriched my life: I've learned to cook new dishes, picked up money-saving tips, and even made an online friend or two through shared interests. Compared to other social media that mostly shows me photos of people's breakfasts, Reddit actually makes me feel like I'm learning something every time I open it.

instruction: Describe a good decision made by someone you know recently.
response: I'd like to describe a good decision made recently by my close friend Emily, who quit her corporate job in finance to become a full-time photographer. She'd been working at a prestigious investment firm for about six years, earning an impressive salary and, by most conventional measures, doing extremely well for herself. But behind the scenes, she was deeply unhappy. She'd always been passionate about photography — she'd carry her camera everywhere on weekends, and her social media was full of stunning shots she'd taken — but she'd convinced herself that photography was just a hobby, too risky to pursue seriously. The turning point came about a year ago, when her workload grew so punishing that she was regularly working ten-hour days and canceling plans with friends. She told me later that she'd sat down one evening and asked herself a brutally honest question: if she carried on like this for another decade, would she look back with pride or with regret? The answer was obvious. So after months of careful planning — saving up a financial cushion, building a client base on the side, and taking professional courses — she handed in her resignation. Honestly, at the time, quite a few of us worried it was reckless. Walking away from a stable career in a tough economy sounded like something out of a movie rather than real life. But her decision has turned out brilliantly. Within her first year, she built a solid reputation specialising in portrait and event photography, and she's now fully booked months in advance. More importantly, the transformation in her is remarkable — she's more energetic, more confident, and genuinely happier than I've seen her in years. What I admire most is that her decision wasn't impulsive at all; it was thoroughly researched and bravely executed. Her example taught me a valuable lesson: that careful planning and courage together can turn a 'risky' decision into the best one you've ever made, and that job security means very little if it costs you your happiness.

topic: a subject to learn in the future
instruction: Describe something/a subject you want to/would like to learn in the future.
response: Something I'm really keen to learn in the future is graphic design, and I've been seriously considering it for a while now. My interest was sparked about a year ago when I volunteered to help a friend promote a small charity event. I ended up making the posters and social media graphics myself, and while the results were admittedly amateurish, I found the process absolutely fascinating — experimenting with colours, fonts, and layouts to try and communicate a message visually. Since then, I've noticed that design is everywhere in my daily life, and I've started looking at things with a much more critical eye: why certain websites feel pleasant to use, why some advertisements stick in my memory while others are instantly forgettable. What draws me to learning graphic design formally is partly practical and partly personal. On the practical side, these skills would be incredibly useful in today's world — virtually every organisation needs visual content for websites, presentations, marketing materials, and social media, and being able to create or at least intelligently evaluate such content would be a genuine asset in my career. I've already got some rudimentary experience with basic editing software, but I know there's a huge gap between dabbling and doing things properly. That's why I'd want to study it systematically: learning the fundamental principles like typography, colour theory, composition, and visual hierarchy, and getting hands-on with industry-standard tools like Photoshop and Illustrator. There are actually some excellent online courses available now, so I'm planning to enrol in one during my free time next year, perhaps dedicating a couple of evenings a week to it. Beyond the career benefits, I think it would be a wonderfully creative outlet — a way to switch off from work while still producing something tangible and beautiful. Ultimately, I'd love to reach the point where I can confidently design things that people genuinely enjoy looking at, and maybe one day even take on freelance projects of my own.

instruction: Describe a daily routine you do.
response: The daily routine I'd like to describe is my morning meditation practice, which I've been following for about a year now and which has honestly transformed my days. It all started after I read several articles about the benefits of mindfulness for mental health. At the time, I was going through a particularly stressful period at work — constantly anxious, sleeping badly, and feeling like my mind was permanently racing — so I figured I had nothing to lose by giving it a try. The routine itself is fairly simple. I wake up at around six thirty, drink a glass of warm water, and then settle into a comfortable spot by my bedroom window, which catches the early morning light. I do twenty minutes of guided meditation using an app on my phone, focusing on my breathing and quietly observing my thoughts without getting swept up in them. In the beginning, it was honestly a struggle — my mind would wander off within seconds, and I'd catch myself mentally writing my to-do list instead of meditating. I nearly gave up several times during the first few weeks. But I persisted, and somewhere around the second month, something shifted. I started noticing that I was reacting to stressful situations more calmly, that the constant background hum of worry in my head had quietened down, and that I was sleeping more soundly at night. What I appreciate most about the routine is how it anchors the rest of my day. Because I do it first thing, before checking any messages or emails, I begin each morning with a sense of clarity and intention rather than immediately feeling bombarded by other people's demands. These days, I genuinely look forward to it — it's become something of a sacred pocket of calm in an otherwise busy schedule. On the rare mornings when I skip it, I can really feel the difference; I'm more irritable and scattered. It's remarkable that something requiring just twenty minutes and no equipment at all can have such a profound effect, and I can't see myself ever giving it up.

instruction: Describe a time when you heard good news (from someone with a good relationship).
response: I'd like to talk about a time when I heard some wonderful news from my best friend, Sarah, which remains one of my happiest memories in recent years. It happened a few months ago on an otherwise completely ordinary afternoon. I was at home, buried in work, when my phone rang and I saw her name on the screen. Even before she said a word, I could tell from her voice that something big had happened — she was practically vibrating with excitement. She'd just been accepted into the master's programme at one of the top universities in the country, the very one she'd been dreaming about for years. Now, some background: Sarah had applied the previous year and been rejected, which had knocked her confidence badly. She'd spent months doubting herself, wondering whether she was good enough, and there was a real chance she'd give up entirely. But instead, she'd spent the year strengthening her application — gaining relevant work experience, retaking a qualification, and rewriting her personal statement from scratch. So when the acceptance email arrived, all that effort had finally paid off, and I was honestly as thrilled as she was, if not more so. I remember jumping up from my desk and pacing around the room as she read out the email, both of us laughing and, I'll admit, both of us getting a bit teary-eyed. She was the first person to achieve something like this in her family, which made it even more meaningful. What made hearing it from her directly so special was that I'd witnessed the whole journey — every moment of doubt, every late night of preparation — so the news felt like a shared victory. We celebrated that weekend with dinner at her favourite restaurant. Reflecting on it now, that phone call reminded me how joyful it is to celebrate a friend's success as if it were your own, and it also reinforced a lesson about perseverance: sometimes a 'no' is just a detour, not a dead end.

instruction: Describe a time when you missed or were late for an important meeting/event.
response: I'd like to describe a time when I was late for something genuinely important — a job interview for a position I'd been dreaming about for months. It happened last year, and even now, just thinking about it makes my stomach flip. The interview was scheduled for ten o'clock in the morning at the company's head office, which was about an hour away from my home. I'm usually a very punctual person — I'd set two alarms, laid out my clothes the night before, and even planned to catch an earlier train than necessary. What could possibly go wrong, right? Well, plenty, as it turned out. That morning, the first alarm failed to go off — later I discovered my phone had updated overnight and somehow silenced it — and I woke up to my second alarm with barely enough time to get ready. I dashed out of the house, skipping breakfast, only to find the roads gridlocked because of an accident on the main route. So I made a snap decision to abandon the bus and take the metro instead, but when I reached the station, I saw the dreaded announcement: significant delays on my line due to a signal failure. I stood there on the platform, in my best suit, sweating and frantically calculating whether I could make it on time, while sending increasingly panicked messages to the HR coordinator. In the end, I arrived twenty-five minutes late, flustered, with my shirt creased and my composure in tatters. To my relief, the interviewers were surprisingly understanding — they'd seen the traffic chaos on the news — and the interview itself actually went reasonably well. Unfortunately, I didn't get the job, though they kindly told me I'd been a strong candidate. The whole experience taught me some valuable lessons: I now build generous buffers into my schedule for anything important, I keep a backup plan in mind, and I always double-check my alarms. It was an awful morning, but honestly, it made me better prepared for everything since.

instruction: Describe a time when you showed something new to others (e.g. family or friends).
response: I'd like to talk about the time I taught my younger brother to ride a bicycle, which was a small event but one that left a lasting impression on both of us. He was about seven at the time, and he'd been begging for a bike for months. When our parents finally bought him one for his birthday, everyone assumed Dad would be the one to teach him — but Dad was away on a business trip, and my brother was far too impatient to wait, so the task fell to me. To be honest, I hadn't realised how challenging it would be. We started out in the empty car park behind our apartment building early on a Saturday morning. I began with the basics: adjusting his helmet, lowering the seat so his feet could touch the ground, and letting him scoot around to get a feel for the balance. The first few attempts at actual pedalling were, frankly, comedy gold — he'd wobble violently for two seconds and then topple over, usually into me. He scraped his knee a couple of times, and I could see his eyes welling up, but what impressed me was his determination. Rather than quitting, he'd just sniff, pick himself up, and say, 'Again.' I kept encouraging him, telling him that falling was simply part of learning and that every cyclist had gone through exactly the same thing. Then came the breakthrough moment. On the second afternoon, after dozens of failed attempts, I gave him a gentle push, let go of the seat — and he just kept going. Fifty metres, then a hundred, wobbling slightly but staying upright. The look on his face was absolutely priceless: a mixture of terror and pure, unfiltered joy. He rode laps around that car park until the sun went down, shouting 'I'm doing it!' every time he passed me. For me, the proudest part wasn't just that he learned to ride; it was watching him conquer his fear through persistence. It's a memory we still laugh about at family dinners, and I think it's when I first understood the satisfaction of teaching someone something new.

instruction: Describe a time when you took a risk.
response: I'd like to describe the biggest risk I've ever taken, which was leaving my stable job to start my own business about two years ago. Let me give you some context first. I'd been working at a well-established company for several years in a comfortable position — decent salary, predictable routine, and the kind of job security that most people would envy. But deep down, I'd always harboured this dream of building something of my own, and I'd been quietly developing a small online business idea in my spare time for over a year. The dilemma was agonising. On one hand, quitting meant giving up a regular income, health insurance, and the comfort of the familiar — and I had friends and family telling me I was throwing away a perfectly good career. On the other hand, I was haunted by the thought that in ten years' time, I'd still be sitting at the same desk, wondering 'what if?' What finally tipped the scales was that I'd been saving aggressively for two years and had put together enough of a financial cushion to survive at least a year without a salary. Even so, the day I handed in my resignation, my hands were literally trembling. The first few months afterwards were terrifying, I won't lie. There was no guaranteed pay cheque at the end of the month, no colleagues to share the pressure with, and more sleepless nights than I can count wondering whether I'd made a catastrophic mistake. There were moments when business was so slow that I seriously considered crawling back to corporate life. But slowly, the business gained traction — the first real clients came, then repeat customers, then referrals, and within eighteen months it was actually covering my living expenses and growing steadily. Looking back, was it risky? Absolutely. But it was a calculated risk, not a reckless gamble, and that distinction matters. More importantly, it taught me resilience, resourcefulness, and self-belief that no stable job ever could. I genuinely believe that without taking that leap, I'd never have discovered what I'm capable of.

instruction: Describe an occasion that you needed to wear your best clothes.
response: I'd like to talk about an occasion when I had to dress in my very best clothes — my cousin's wedding, which took place about two years ago. It was a grand, traditional ceremony, and the whole family had been preparing for it for months, so there was no question of turning up in anything less than your finest attire. For me, this involved a proper shopping expedition, because honestly, my wardrobe consisted mostly of jeans, T-shirts, and work clothes that weren't remotely suitable for such an occasion. I eventually settled on a tailored dark navy suit with a subtle sheen, a crisp white shirt, a silk tie in deep burgundy, and polished leather shoes — and I have to say, when I tried on the complete outfit, I barely recognised myself in the mirror. The day itself was absolutely sweltering, which made the full suit something of a test of endurance, but I have to admit the effort felt worthwhile. There's something about dressing formally that changes how you carry yourself — I stood a little straighter, felt more confident, and genuinely enjoyed the sense of occasion. The venue was a beautifully decorated hotel ballroom with floral centrepieces, chandeliers, and a stage decked out in red and gold. Everyone looked spectacular, especially my cousin, who wore a stunning traditional gown. Throughout the day there were ceremonial rituals, toasts, speeches, and of course an enormous banquet with what felt like a hundred dishes. What made the occasion memorable beyond the clothes was the atmosphere — relatives I hadn't seen in years had travelled from far away, and there was this wonderful feeling of the whole family coming together to celebrate. We took countless photographs, danced until late in the evening, and laughed until our faces ached. That event taught me that while clothes themselves are just fabric, dressing up for something important is really a way of showing respect and embracing the moment. I still have that suit hanging in my wardrobe, and every time I see it, I'm reminded of that wonderful day.

instruction: Describe a time you got something you wanted.
response: I'd like to describe the time I received something I'd wanted for a very long time — a guitar, given to me by my best friend for my twenty-fifth birthday. To explain why it meant so much, I need to go back a bit. I'd been obsessed with music since my teens, and learning to play the guitar had sat at the top of my wish list for years. I'd linger in music shops, pick up the instruments, and daydream about strumming songs around a campfire, but every time I got close to buying one, something else always took priority — rent, textbooks, unexpected expenses. There was always a reasonable excuse, and the dream kept getting postponed. Then came my birthday. It was a Saturday evening, and a group of close friends had gathered at my flat for what I assumed was a simple dinner. Halfway through the evening, my best friend appeared from the hallway carrying an enormous box wrapped in shiny paper, with an enormous bow on top, and a knowing grin on his face. Even before I'd finished unwrapping it, I'd guessed what it was — my heart was pounding — and when the lid came off and I saw that beautiful acoustic guitar nestled inside, I was genuinely speechless. I'm not exaggerating when I say it's the best gift I've ever received. What touched me most wasn't just the guitar itself, though it was a lovely one with a warm, honey-coloured finish — it was the thoughtfulness behind it. My friend had done his research, read reviews, visited several shops, and even asked my family about my preferences, all to make sure he got it right. That level of care meant the world to me. True to my word, I threw myself into learning — I took lessons, practised daily, and six months later I played a full song at another friend's gathering to genuine applause. That gift didn't just give me an instrument; it gave me a hobby that's brought me endless joy, and it deepened a friendship I'll always treasure.

instruction: Describe an enjoyable journey by public transport.
response: I'd like to describe one of the most enjoyable journeys I've ever taken — a train trip from my hometown to Edinburgh with my family a couple of years ago. We could easily have flown, but on a friend's recommendation we decided to take the train, and it turned out to be one of the best travel decisions we've ever made. The journey took about four and a half hours, which might sound long, but honestly, it flew by. We'd booked seats in a carriage with large panoramic windows, and the scenery along the way was simply spectacular — rolling green hills dotted with sheep, stone villages with smoke curling from chimneys, ancient castles perched on hillsides, and rivers winding through valleys. I spent the first hour just gazing out of the window, and I wasn't alone; even my phone-obsessed younger brother was glued to the glass. What made the trip so pleasant was how relaxed everything felt compared to flying. There was no tense rush to the airport, no security queues, no cramped seats with knees pressed against the seat in front. We could spread out, wander to the dining car for coffee and snacks, play card games, and chat freely the whole way. My dad, who's a history enthusiast, turned the journey into an impromptu lecture, pointing out landmarks and telling us stories about the places we passed through, which made the landscape come alive. Another thing I loved was the sense of anticipation that builds on a train journey — unlike a flight, where you're sealed in a metal tube and suddenly spat out at your destination, a train feels like a gradual transition, with the scenery slowly changing character as you travel north. When Edinburgh finally came into view, with its dramatic skyline and the castle looming over the city, it felt like a fitting climax to the journey itself. That trip convinced me that the journey can be just as wonderful as the destination, and ever since, I've actively chosen trains over planes whenever the distance allows.

instruction: Describe a time you did something that made you feel proud.
response: I'd like to talk about a time I felt genuinely proud of myself — when I organised a charity fundraiser at my university during my final year. It came about when a group of friends and I learned about a local children's hospital that was struggling to upgrade its equipment. We wanted to help, but none of us had much money to donate, so we decided instead to organise a charity event — a talent show and flea market on campus — and donate all the proceeds. What I didn't fully appreciate at the time was just how much work organising such an event would involve. As the person coordinating everything, I had to get permission from the university administration, which meant weeks of emails, forms, and meetings. I had to recruit and manage a team of about fifteen volunteers, contact local businesses to ask for sponsorship and raffle prizes, promote the event through posters and social media, and handle logistics like stalls, sound equipment, and seating. There were plenty of stressful moments — a sponsor pulled out two weeks before the event, two volunteers dropped out during exam season, and it poured with rain on the morning we were setting up the outdoor stalls. I remember standing there in the drizzle, soaked and stressed, wondering if the whole thing would be a disaster. But we adapted, moved everything indoors, and somehow pulled it off. In the end, over three hundred people attended, the talent show was a genuine hit, and we raised a sum far exceeding what we'd hoped for — enough to make a real difference to the hospital's equipment fund. The proudest moment came a few weeks later when we visited the hospital to hand over the cheque and saw the faces of the nurses and children. All the stress evaporated in that instant. Beyond the money raised, the experience taught me leadership, perseverance, and problem-solving under pressure, and it showed me that ordinary students, with no special resources, can still do something meaningful for their community. That sense of accomplishment is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life.
